nodes.statement: Prove both exact infinitude clauses; clause 1 implies clause 2 by ε=1.
ALL-AFFIRMATIVE CLOSE: prove B_1 is infinite and prove ∃ε>0 with B_ε infinite.
A clause-1 negative is B_1 finite.
A clause-2 negative is ∀ε>0, B_ε finite; checking only ε≥1 or one ε does not establish it.
COMPLETE MIXED/NEGATIVE CLOSE: give a complete two-clause truth vector other than YES/YES. The only logically impossible vector is YES/NO; NO/NO and NO/YES are both admissible.

Let $\omega(n)$ count the number of distinct primes dividing $n$. Are there infinitely many $n$ such that, for all $m<n$, we have $m+\omega(m) \leq n$?Can one show that there exists an $\epsilon>0$ such that there are infinitely many $n$ where $m+\epsilon \omega(m)\leq n$ for all $m<n$?
